title: Primary Function of the Shaft
learningObjectives: Identify the shaft's role in the drive system.
student: What is the primary mechanical function of the shaft in the belt-drive system?
instructor: The shaft transfers rotational mechanical power from the motor to the pulley, which transfers the power through the belts to the driven equipment.

title: Power Input and Mechanical Loading
learningObjectives: Relate operating power and speed to torque demand.
student: What operating quantities determine how heavily the shaft is loaded in torsion?
instructor: The transmitted power and rotational speed determine the torsional loading. Greater power increases the torque demand, while lower rotational speed increases torque for the same transmitted power.

title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Interpret the functions of the drive-system components.
student: What are the functions of the motor connection, pulley, and bearing in the physical drive system?
instructor: The motor connection supplies mechanical power and torque to the shaft. The pulley removes torque from the shaft and transfers it to the belts. The bearing supports and aligns the shaft while allowing it to rotate.

title: Torque Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace mechanical power through the drive system.
student: Trace the mechanical power-transfer path from the motor to the driven equipment.
instructor: The load path is motor → drive shaft → pulley → belts → driven equipment.

title: Critical Component and Response
learningObjectives: Identify the response governing the base shaft-sizing model.
student: What mechanical response of the shaft is important when determining whether its diameter is adequate?
instructor: The important response is torsion and the resulting shear stress. For a solid circular shaft, the maximum torsional shear stress occurs at the outer surface, and the diameter must keep that stress below the allowable value.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify the operating, geometric, and material inputs controlling shaft size.
student: What operating, geometric, and material characteristics would you expect to influence the required shaft size?
instructor: The important characteristics are transmitted power, rotational speed, shaft diameter, and allowable torsional shear stress. Power and speed establish torque, diameter controls the resulting stress, and allowable stress sets the design limit.

title: Speed Sensitivity
learningObjectives: Predict how operating speed affects torque and required diameter.
student: For the same transmitted power, would operating the shaft at a lower rotational speed generally require a larger or smaller shaft? Explain qualitatively.
instructor: A lower rotational speed produces greater torque for the same power. The greater torque produces greater torsional shear stress, so a larger shaft is generally required.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the physical system into a simplified torsion model.
student: Convert the real belt-drive system into a simplified torsion model. Show the motor, shaft, pulley, bearing, transmitted torque, shaft diameter, and direction of rotation.
instructor: A valid idealization shows the motor as the torque source, the solid shaft as the torque-carrying member, the pulley as the torque output to the belts, and the bearing as a radial support that permits rotation. The shaft segment between the motor and pulley carries the transmitted internal torque.
gradingNotes: Students should create their own model before viewing the supplied idealized figure.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State the assumptions supporting the base torsion analysis.
student: State the modeling assumptions used for the base shaft analysis.
instructor: Assume steady operation, a solid circular shaft, linear-elastic material behavior, uniform shaft diameter, pure torsion, negligible shaft self-weight, negligible bearing friction, and constant transmitted power. Belt-induced bending, keyways, stress concentrations, shock, and fatigue are excluded from the base model.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the complete stress-based shaft selection.
student: Outline the mechanics-analysis procedure before substituting numerical values.
instructor: Convert rotational speed from rpm to rad/s, calculate torque from power and angular speed, identify the maximum internal torque, apply the solid-shaft torsional shear-stress equation, solve for the minimum diameter, round upward to the next standard size, and verify the stress in the selected shaft.

title: Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Interpret the torsional boundary conditions from the idealized model.
student: Using the idealized model, identify where torque enters and leaves the shaft and explain the role of bearing B.
instructor: Torque enters the shaft at A from the motor and is removed at the pulley by the belt drive. Bearing B provides radial support and permits rotation; it is not modeled as a torsional restraint.

title: Angular Speed
learningObjectives: Convert rotational speed to angular speed.
student: Convert the assigned shaft speed from rpm to rad/s.

title: Transmitted Torque
learningObjectives: Calculate shaft torque from power and speed.
student: Determine the torque carried by the shaft from the specified motor power and operating speed.
instructor: Convert the motor power using 1 hp = 550 ft·lb/s: P = ({{P}} hp)(550 ft·lb/s per hp). Then T = P/ω = {{shaft_torque_lb_ft}} lb·ft = {{shaft_torque_lb_in}} lb·in.
commonMistakes: Use lb·in when combining torque with a shaft diameter measured in inches.

title: Internal Torque Diagram
student: Draw and label the internal torque diagram for the idealized drive shaft.
instructor: The shaft segment between the motor and pulley carries a constant internal torque of {{shaft_torque_lb_ft}} lb·ft. The segment between the pulley and bearing carries approximately zero internal torque because the bearing does not provide a torsional reaction.

title: Minimum Theoretical Diameter
learningObjectives: Solve the torsion relation for minimum shaft diameter.
student: Using the allowable torsional shear stress, determine the minimum theoretical diameter of the solid circular shaft.
instructor: For a solid circular shaft, τmax = 16T/(πd3). Therefore, dmin = [16T/(πτallow)]1/3 = {{shaft_d_min_in}} in.

title: Standard Shaft Selection
learningObjectives: Select the next appropriate standard shaft diameter.
student: Select the smallest appropriate standard shaft diameter in 1/8-in increments and explain why the size must be rounded upward.
instructor: The minimum theoretical diameter is {{shaft_d_min_in}} in, so select the next larger 1/8-in size: {{shaft_d_selected_label}} ({{shaft_d_selected_in}} in). The next lower standard size, {{shaft_d_lower_in}} in, is below the theoretical minimum and is not acceptable.

title: Selected-Diameter Verification
learningObjectives: Verify the torsional stress in the selected shaft.
student: Calculate the actual maximum torsional shear stress in the selected shaft and compare it with the allowable stress.
gradingNotes: The cleaned faculty solution reports approximately 13.70 ksi; small differences reflect rounding of intermediate torque values.

title: Utilization and Margin
learningObjectives: Quantify how closely the selected shaft approaches the stress limit.
student: Determine the stress-utilization ratio and allowable-stress factor for the selected shaft.
instructor: Utilization = τactual/τallow = {{shaft_utilization}}. The allowable-stress factor is τallow/τactual = {{shaft_allowable_factor}}. The selected size passes, but the margin is modest.
gradingNotes: The cleaned faculty solution gives approximately 0.945 utilization and 1.058 allowable-stress factor; results based on unrounded intermediate values are approximately 0.944 and 1.059.

title: Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: Make a bounded recommendation and identify omitted effects.
student: State whether the selected shaft is acceptable for the base model and identify additional effects that should be checked in a detailed design.
instructor:
{{shaft_recommendation}}

Detailed design should also consider belt-induced bending, bearing reactions, keyways and stress concentrations, shock loading, fatigue, critical speed, coupling details, and manufacturing tolerances.
gradingNotes: Students should not claim complete system safety from the simplified steady pure-torsion calculation alone.
